operative_text.controlling:
2.14(1)  If an individual or estate who is required to have a
litigation representative under rule 2.11 does not have one, an
interested person
(a) may file an affidavit in Form 1 containing the information
described in subrule (2), and by doing so becomes the
litigation representative for that individual or estate, and
(b) where an interested person has, or proposes to, become
the litigation representative under clause (a) for an estate,
the interested person must serve notice of the appointment
in Form 2 on the beneficiaries and heirs at law of the
deceased.
(2)  The affidavit must include
(a) the interested person’s agreement in writing to be the
litigation representative,
(b) the reason for the self-appointment,
(c) the relationship between the litigation representative and
the individual or estate the litigation representative will
represent,
(d) a statement that the litigation representative has no
interest in the action adverse in interest to the party the
litigation representative will represent,
(e) if the litigation representative is an individual, a statement
that the litigation representative is a resident of Alberta,
(f) if the litigation representative is a corporation, the place of
business or activity of the corporation in Alberta, and
(g) an acknowledgment of potential liability for payment of a
costs award attributable to or liable to be paid by the
litigation representative.
(3)  If a person proposes to become a self-appointed litigation
representative for the estate of a deceased person, the affidavit
referred to in subrule (2) must, in addition to the matters set out in
subrule (2), disclose any of the following matters that apply:
(a) whether the estate has a substantial interest in the action
or proposed action;
(b) whether the litigation representative has or may have
duties to perform in the administration of the estate of the
deceased;
(c) whether an application has been or will be made for
administration of the estate of the deceased;
(d) whether the litigation representative does or may represent
interests adverse to any other party in the action or
proposed action;
(e) repealed AR 143/2011 s2.
(4)  A person proposing to become a self-appointed litigation
representative has no authority to make or defend a claim or,
without the Court’s permission, to make an application or take any
proceeding in an action, until the affidavit referred to in subrule
(1)(a) is filed.

BOOK_A.title: Self-appointed Litigation Representatives
BOOK_A.commentary:
Previously a person could self-appoint as a “next friend” of a party. This Rule expands the
circumstances under which someone can unilaterally sue or defend for another, and establishes
a procedure for doing so.
This Rule does not let one lay person speak for another litigant who is not under a disability.¹
The court can decide who will be a litigation representative for someone else, and ended here
the appointment of such a litigation representative. Only suitable persons should so act. One can
self-appoint only if the individual or estate was required to have a litigation representative. But this
estate already had one. And the afﬁdavit required had never been ﬁled.²

Rule 2.14 is novel, and raises more questions than it answers, especially as it does not deﬁne
"interested". If this Rule is properly conceived, it is poorly drafted. Does "interested" mean "want to
talk about or litigate this topic", or "have a legally-enforceable right", or "claim a legal right though
that is disputed"? The last of the 3 meanings was in effect adopted.¹
A person can validly self-appoint without having any particular (or the stated) status?²
In any
event, the afﬁdavit under R.2.14 by the self-appointee only need give that person's "reasons for
self-appointing".³
Where no one applies for letters of administration (or probate) of a deceased person's estate,
and the only other person who wishes to apply has a conﬂict of interest, that is a weighty reason
for someone else self-appointing to represent the estate?⁴

footnotes.text: Nahirney v. Ogilvie & Co. , supra, R.2.13n.
Royal Bank of Can. v. Godbout 2021 ABQB 191, JCRD 2010 00857 (Mar 11) (¶’s 12-19).
while denying any need to adopt a deﬁnition, in Kunkel v. Winquist 2022 ABQB 367, JCE 2003 13470 (May 24).
even if they may have a similar conﬂict? Kunkel v. Winquist, supra (¶ 38).

BOOK_A.commentary_review_flag: 5th pass: 'the affidavit under R.2.14 by the self-appointee only need give that person's "reasons for self-appointing"' (p.2-38, Kunkel para 31) is about proving status; read literally it is narrower than official 2.14(2)-(3), which require agreement in writing, the reason, the relationship, no adverse interest, residence or place of business, a costs acknowledgment, and (for estates) the (3)(a)-(d) disclosures.

BOOK_B.title: Self-appointed litigation representatives

commentary.text: Rule 2.14 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 2.14. An Estate Requires Representation to Appear in Court In Oommen v. Ramjohn, 2015 ABCA 34, 2015 CarswellAlta 102, 3 E.T.R. (4th) 207, Mr. Oommen, one of the named co-executors in a will not yet probated, “appointed himself the estate's litigation representative pursuant to Rule 2.14”, and now wished to represent (without counsel) the estate in the Court of Queen's Bench in relation to a judgment the deceased had obtained before his death. In an Application for Incidental Direction, Madam Justice Veldhuis held he could not do so without legal counsel. Her Ladyship said, at paragraphs 3-4: 3 The Rules of Court provide that individuals may represent themselves in an action: Rule 2.22. An estate is not an individual in this context but a separate legal entity. This has been established in the constitutional context: Stinson (Estate of) v British Columbia, 1999 BCCA 761 at para 15, 133 BCAC 15; Canada (Attorney General) v Hislop, 2007 SCC 10 at para 73, [2007] 1 SCR 429. In addition, Rule 2.14(1) refers to an “individual or estate” (emphasis added), indicating the two concepts are distinct. 4 An estate therefore requires representation to appear in court. Section 106(1) of the Legal Profession Act, RSA 2000, c L-8 provides that no person shall commence, carry on or defend an action or proceeding before a court or judge on another's behalf unless that person is an active member of the Law Society of Alberta. Section 106(2) provides a number of exceptions to this rule, none of which apply in the circumstances of this case.

information_notes.text:
For the liability of a litigation representative to pay a costs award, see rule 10.47 [Liability of
litigation representative for costs].

see_also: BOOK_A other Parts (full Book A uploaded; 6th pass): R.3.74 notes (p.3-243) refer to 'Rr.2.11 to 2.16'. Official, by subject: 10.47 - a plaintiff's litigation representative is liable for costs; a defendant's only for serious misconduct and by order (the costs acknowledgment in 2.14(2)(g)).
BOOK_B 2.22 commentary quotes the same Oommen v Ramjohn passage as BOOK_B 2.14.

Cross-book (4th pass): Oommen v. Ramjohn 2015 ABCA 34 is also BOOK_A 2.22 fn 8 (p.2-45, 'Oommen (Chapman Est.) v. Ramjohn'). Kunkel v. Winquist 2022 ABQB 367 (BOOK_A 2.14 fns p.2-38) is also cited by BOOK_B under 2.11 and by BOOK_A and BOOK_C under 2.21 (wording corrected in 5th pass - BOOK_A does not cite it under 2.11). BOOK_A fn 2 'Royal Bank of Can. v. Godbout 2021 ABQB 191' and BOOK_A 2.21 fn 4 'Royal Bank v. Godbout 2021 ABQB 321' are two different decisions in the same court file. BOOK_A 2.11 fn 10 cites '2.14(2)(f)' for costs - probably 2.14(2)(g) (flagged under 2.11).

Official Form 1 is headed '[Rule 2.14]' (the affidavit named in 2.14(1)(a)) and Form 2 '[Rule 2.14(1)(b)]' (notice of appointment to beneficiaries and heirs). Form 1 was found in the 4th pass of 2.21-2.32; Form 2 was missed by that search pattern (it has a subrule in the heading) and added in the 5th pass.
